title: Observed in the bathroom
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on an inpatient psychiatric ward. Ms Reid, 24, is on close observation, with a member of staff within arm's length at all times, after self-harming on the ward last week.

She tells you, distressed, that a male healthcare assistant has been observing her in the bathroom and while she showers. She says she feels humiliated and has stopped washing.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Tell the staff to stop observing her in the bathroom.
options.brief: Could leave her at risk at a time when she may self-harm.
options.detailed: Bathrooms can be high-risk places for self-harm. Stopping observation there without a risk review could be dangerous.

options.text: Explain that close observation is ward policy and must continue.
options.brief: Ignores a legitimate concern about her dignity.
options.detailed: Observation may need to continue, but how it is done matters. Dismissing her concern doesn't help.

options.text: Ask the nurse in charge for female staff to observe her.
options.brief: A same-sex observer respects her dignity while keeping her safe.
options.detailed: Close observation can still respect privacy. Allocating female staff for her personal care, wherever possible, keeps her safe without the humiliation she describes.

options.text: Talk with her about how the observation is affecting her.
options.brief: Her experience matters and helps the team plan her care.
options.detailed: She has stopped washing, which affects her health and dignity. Listening to her helps the team understand what would make observation more bearable.

options.text: Suggest the assistant stands outside the bathroom with the door ajar.
options.brief: A possible compromise, but not your decision to make alone.
options.detailed: This may be reasonable if her risk allows, but changing how observation works should be agreed by the team, not arranged informally.

options.text: Record her complaint in the notes and take no further action.
options.brief: Documentation alone doesn't address her distress.
options.detailed: Her concern should be recorded, but she needs something to change.

options.text: Ask the team to review whether this level of observation is needed.
options.brief: Observation should be the least restrictive level that keeps her safe.
options.detailed: Observation levels should be reviewed regularly. If her risk has reduced, a less intrusive level may be appropriate. If not, the team can look at how it is carried out.

options.text: Advise her to make a formal complaint to the ward manager.
options.brief: She can complain, but the problem needs addressing now.
options.detailed: She has the right to complain, but this puts the burden on her and doesn't solve the immediate problem.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you protect a patient's dignity while respecting the safety reasons for her observation.
explanation.keyDetails: She is on close observation after self-harm. A male member of staff observes her personal care. She is distressed and has stopped washing.
explanation.reasoning: [C] arranges female observers, [D] listens to her, and [G] reviews whether the level is still right. The distractors remove safety measures ([A]), dismiss her ([B], [F]), change practice informally ([E]), or shift the burden ([H]).
explanation.competing: [E] may well be where the team ends up, but changes to observation should be agreed by the team after a risk review.

references.title: Equality Act 2010
references.note: Same-sex care and respecting patients' privacy.
